results.title: Better decision making through objective numeracy and ...
results.content: Numeric self-efficacy (i.e., self-reported numeric confidence) also has psychologically distinct influences in decision-making processes related to numeric-task persistence and emotional reactions; it appears to motivate the use of numeric ability critical to health and financial success. In the present chapter, we focus on the psychological mechanisms underlying the impacts of numeric knowledge and skills (i.e., objective numeracy, which is like literacy but with numbers) and numeric self-efficacy (i.e., numeric confidence) in judgment and decision making. The effects of objective numeracy, numeric self-efficacy, and other metacognitive measures have been incorporated into influential dual-process theories as variables that increase the likelihood of superior decisions and/or more effortful cognitive processes (e.g., Reyna, Nelson, Han, & Dieckmann, 2009; Stanovich, 2018). Similar to the work on “boosting” (Hertwig & Grüne-Yanoff, 2017), our numeracy research turned early on to how we can help people take charge of their own lives, by increasing objective numeracy long-term through education and by increasing numeric understanding and use in decisions through evidence-based information presentation (e.g., Peters et al., 2007).
